steps.title: Too good to be true
steps.html:
Three stories that millions of people believed. One took forty years to unravel; another lasted a single afternoon.

A  In December 1912 a lawyer named Charles Dawson announced that he had found something remarkable in a gravel pit in the south of England: a skull with a human forehead and an ape-like jaw. Scientists were keen to find evidence that would prove the link between early man and apes, and here it was. The find was reported around the world. Museums put it on display. It was named Piltdown Man.

B  By the time the hoax was discovered, scientists had wasted nearly forty years believing a lie. In 1953 a team of researchers tested the bones properly and reached an uncomfortable conclusion: the skull was human and modern, the jaw belonged to an orangutan, and the teeth had been filed down and stained to match. Meanwhile Dawson, who most people now consider responsible for making the fake, had died. Nobody was ever charged.

C  Not every hoax takes forty years. On 15 October 2009 the media reported that a six-year-old boy was inside a large silver balloon floating high in the sky above Colorado. The police were informed and helicopters were sent up to track it. By the time the balloon finally landed about eighty kilometres away, an hour or so later, the story was live on television and millions of people were watching.

D  The boy was not in the balloon. He was at home, hiding in the family garage. That evening, while reporters were interviewing the family on live television, he accidentally mentioned that they had done it “for the show”. The whole story had been made up by his parents in an attempt to get a reality TV deal. As soon as the interview ended, the police reopened the case.

E  Hoaxes travel faster than they used to. Before the internet, a false story needed a newspaper. Now a picture circulates in minutes: a bright blue watermelon that supposedly changes the taste of everything you eat afterwards, or a claim that dialling the emergency number will charge your phone battery. That second one caused real harm. Police announced that calls to 999 had risen sharply, and told the public to ignore the hoax and keep the line free.

F  So why do we believe? Researchers who study this point to two things. First, a good hoax gives people what they already expect — Piltdown Man arrived exactly when scientists were looking for it. Second, checking takes effort, and sharing takes none. Until that changes, the next story that seems too good to be true will still reach a few million screens before anyone thinks to ask.
